title: 03 · Wikipedia Tables and AI-Assisted ETV Flows
text:
The question

Which decade produced the most of the 50 highest-grossing films of all time?

Write your guess down. (Hint: think about when ticket prices and global releases grew.)

title: 03 · Wikipedia Tables and AI-Assisted ETV Flows
section: CSV vs. HTML: what’s different about Extract
text:
CSV vs. HTML: what’s different about Extract
In file 02 the data was already a table in a file built for computers. A web page is built for humans: the table you see is wrapped in HTML tags, mixed in with headings, images, footnotes, and navigation. Extracting it means:

Downloading the page (all of it, not just the table).
Finding the right table among several on the page.
Reading the cells and reconstructing rows and columns, including cells that span multiple rows or columns.
Cleaning out footnote markers, citation numbers, and formatting that was meant for eyes, not math.

read_csv() does none of this because a CSV needs none of it. htmltab() does steps 1–3 for you and some of step 4. The rest of the cleaning is on you, which is why checking your result matters even more here.

title: 03 · Wikipedia Tables and AI-Assisted ETV Flows
text:
The page
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_films
The first table on the page lists the top 50 films by worldwide box-office gross (not adjusted for inflation). Its columns, as shown on the page: Rank, Peak, Title, Worldwide gross, Year, Ref. Titles of films still in theaters carry a dagger (†).






WarningThis table changes



Wikipedia updates this list as films are released. The numbers in your extract will differ from the backup CSV and from the checkpoints below. The structure and the code are what matter. The backup data/top_films_backup.csv was saved on 2026-10-28.

title: 03 · Wikipedia Tables and AI-Assisted ETV Flows
text:
EXTRACT — htmltab
Add the package to your script and extract. We select the table with an XPath expression that means “the first table on the page with the CSS class wikitable.” This skips any sidebar or navigation tables and is more robust than guessing a table number.
library(htmltab)

films_url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_films"

top_films <- htmltab(
  doc   = films_url,
  which = "//table[contains(@class, 'wikitable')][1]"
)
Checkpoint:
dim(top_films)      # expect 50 rows; 5 or 6 columns
names(top_films)    # expect "Rank" "Peak" "Title" "Worldwide gross" "Year" (maybe "Ref")
glimpse(top_films)
Two things to notice in glimpse():

Every column is chr (text), even Rank and Year. htmltab doesn’t guess types; it hands you the cell text. We’ll convert.
htmltab removes superscript citation markers by default, so the Ref column may come through empty and be dropped, or it may survive as an empty column. Either way we won’t use it.







ImportantIf htmltab fails (no internet, package didn’t install, Wikipedia changed)



Use the backup. The column names are identical, so every line of code below works unchanged:
top_films <- read_csv("data/top_films_backup.csv")
One difference: read_csv() will guess that Rank, Peak, and Year are numbers while Worldwide gross stays text. The cleaning code below handles both cases.

title: 03 · Wikipedia Tables and AI-Assisted ETV Flows
section: TRANSFORM — two cleaning steps and a decade column
text:
TRANSFORM — two cleaning steps and a decade column
Cleaning step 1: numbers stored as text. "$2,937,323,455" is text. parse_number() (readr) strips the $ and commas. Rank and Year are plain digits, so as.numeric() is enough and works whether they arrived as text (htmltab) or already-numeric (backup CSV).
Cleaning step 2: footnote markers. The dagger on "Avengers: Endgame †" is information (still in theaters), so rather than deleting it we record it as its own TRUE/FALSE column, then strip it from the title. grepl() tests whether a pattern appears; gsub() replaces it; trimws() removes leftover spaces.
films_clean <- top_films |>
  select(Rank, Peak, Title, `Worldwide gross`, Year) |>   # drops Ref if present
  mutate(
    rank        = as.numeric(Rank),
    year        = as.numeric(Year),
    gross       = parse_number(`Worldwide gross`),
    in_theaters = grepl("†", Title),
    title       = trimws(gsub("†", "", Title)),
    decade      = floor(year / 10) * 10
  ) |>
  select(rank, title, year, decade, gross, in_theaters)
Why backticks around `Worldwide gross`? Column names with spaces need them. Our new names are lowercase with underscores so we never need backticks again.
Why floor(year / 10) * 10? 2015 / 10 = 201.5, floor → 201, × 10 → 2010. Every year from 2010 to 2019 lands on 2010. Remember this line; it comes back in the AI section.
Checkpoint:
glimpse(films_clean)
Six columns; rank, year, decade, gross are dbl; in_theaters is lgl. Then:
films_clean |>
  select(title, gross, decade, in_theaters) |>
  head(5)



title
gross
decade
in_theaters




Avengers: Endgame
2937323455
2010
TRUE


Avatar
2923710708
2000
FALSE


…






summary(films_clean$gross)   # min ≈ 1.06e9, max ≈ 2.9e9, no NAs
sum(is.na(films_clean$year)) # 0
If gross has NAs, a row’s text didn’t parse. Look at it: films_clean |> filter(is.na(gross)).

title: 03 · Wikipedia Tables and AI-Assisted ETV Flows
text:
TRANSFORM — count films per decade
films_by_decade <- films_clean |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(
    films     = n(),
    avg_gross = mean(gross)
  )

films_by_decade
Checkpoint (backup CSV, saved 2026-10-28):
  decade films   avg_gross
   <dbl> <int>       <dbl>
1   1990     1 2257906828
2   2000     3 1712629293
3   2010    32 1354249742
4   2020    14 1691370099
The row counts should add to 50. If they add to 49 or 51, a row was lost or duplicated in cleaning.

title: 03 · Wikipedia Tables and AI-Assisted ETV Flows
text:
VISUALIZE
ggplot(films_by_decade, aes(x = factor(decade), y = films)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3b4f8c") +
  labs(
    title    = "The 2010s dominate the all-time top 50",
    subtitle = "Number of films among the 50 highest-grossing (not inflation-adjusted)",
    x        = "Decade",
    y        = "Films in the top 50",
    caption  = "Source: Wikipedia, List of highest-grossing films (retrieved 2026-10-28)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
factor(decade) tells ggplot to treat decades as labeled categories (so you get bars labeled 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020) rather than as a continuous number line with awkward gaps.
Checkpoint: four bars; 2010 towers over the rest at 32.
Plain-language answer: Of the 50 highest-grossing films, 32 (64%) were released in the 2010s, 14 in the 2020s, 3 in the 2000s, and just one (Titanic) in the 1990s. This is a list of unadjusted dollars, so it tilts toward recent years when ticket prices were higher and international markets larger. It tells us which era sold the most dollars of tickets, not which era made the most beloved films. Note also that the 2020s count is still growing; four films on the list are still in theaters.

title: 03 · Wikipedia Tables and AI-Assisted ETV Flows
text:
AI-assisted ETV flows
You’ve just done an ETV cycle by hand. Now you’ll use an AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, or similar) to do the next cycle faster, without giving up control of whether the answer is right.
The flow is always:
Question → transformation plan → R code → checks → visualization → interpretation
The AI is good at the middle (plan, code). You own the ends (the question, and deciding whether the result actually answers it) and the checks in between. Never paste AI code and run it all at once. Run it one pipe step at a time and look at what comes out.

Step 1: you do a small one yourself (3 minutes)
New question: Of the films still in theaters, which has the highest gross?
Write it with what you know: filter(), arrange(), desc(). (Answer: a one-row or few-row table, sorted.)
films_clean |>
  filter(in_theaters) |>
  arrange(desc(gross))
Four rows (as of the backup); Spider-Man: Brand New Day on top. Easy. The point is that you decided the steps.


Step 2: the prompt template
Copy this into your AI tool and fill in the brackets. Every bracket exists for a reason: the AI cannot see your data, so you have to describe it precisely, and you need to constrain it so it doesn’t invent columns or quietly drop rows.
I am working in R with a data frame named `films_clean`. Please help me answer this question:

QUESTION: [your question here]

DATA FRAME: films_clean (50 rows). Columns and types:
- rank: numeric (1 to 50)
- title: character
- year: numeric (release year, e.g. 2019)
- decade: numeric (1990, 2000, 2010, 2020; computed as floor(year/10)*10)
- gross: numeric (worldwide gross in US dollars, e.g. 2937323455)
- in_theaters: logical (TRUE if the film is still in release)

SAMPLE ROWS (first 3):
rank  title              year  decade  gross       in_theaters
1     Avengers: Endgame  2019  2010    2937323455  TRUE
2     Avatar             2009  2000    2923710708  FALSE
3     Spider-Man: Brand New Day  2026  2020  2512865567  TRUE

CONSTRAINTS:
- Use only base R plus the packages readr, dplyr, and ggplot2. Do not load tidyverse or other packages.
- Use the native pipe |> (not %>%).
- Do not invent columns that are not listed above.
- There are no missing values. Do not add na.rm or filter out NAs unless I ask.
- Do not change the number of rows unless the question requires it, and if it does, say so.

PLEASE RESPOND IN THIS ORDER:
1. A plain-language transformation plan (2 to 5 numbered steps) BEFORE any code.
2. The R code, built one pipe step at a time with a short comment per step.
3. Check code I can run to verify: the row count after each filter or group, any NAs introduced, the groups that were created, and the final summary table.
4. A ggplot2 chart whose title states the answer.
5. One sentence stating what the result means in plain language and one limitation.


Step 3: use AI to extend the analysis (6 minutes)
Your new question: Which decade had the highest average gross among the top 50, and is the leading decade also the one with the most films?
Paste the template with that question. Below is an example of a plausible AI response. Read it before you run anything. It contains one mistake.






NoteExample AI response (contains an error; find it)





Transformation plan

Start from films_clean (50 rows).
Group the films by decade.
For each decade compute the number of films and the mean of gross.
Sort the result so the highest average gross is first.
Plot average gross by decade as a bar chart.

Code
decade_avg <- films_clean |>
  mutate(decade = round(year, -1)) |>          # bucket each year into its decade
  group_by(decade) |>                          # one group per decade
  summarise(
    films     = n(),                           # how many films
    avg_gross = mean(gross)                    # average worldwide gross
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_gross))                     # highest average first

decade_avg
Checks
nrow(films_clean)                 # 50, unchanged
sum(is.na(decade_avg$avg_gross))  # 0
sum(decade_avg$films)             # should be 50
decade_avg                        # inspect the groups
Chart
ggplot(decade_avg, aes(x = factor(decade), y = avg_gross / 1e9)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3b4f8c") +
  labs(
    title = "Average gross per top-50 film, by decade",
    x = "Decade", y = "Average gross (billions USD)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
Interpretation
The decade with the highest average gross is the one at the top of decade_avg. Limitation: these are unadjusted dollars, so later decades are inflated by higher ticket prices.





Step 4: find and fix the mistake (3 minutes)
Run the code one step at a time. After the mutate() line, look at the result:
films_clean |>
  mutate(decade_ai = round(year, -1)) |>
  select(title, year, decade, decade_ai) |>
  filter(decade != decade_ai)
Something is wrong. round(year, -1) rounds to the nearest ten, so 2015 becomes 2020 and 2005 becomes 2010. That isn’t a decade; it’s a rounding bucket. Films from 2015–2019 get moved into the “2020s.” The films column will still sum to 50 (so that check passes!), and there are no NAs (that check passes too), yet the groups are wrong. The check that catches it is the one the template asked for: inspect the groups that were created, and compare against a column you already trust.
The fix is the line you already wrote earlier in this file:
decade_avg <- films_clean |>
  group_by(decade) |>                 # use the decade column we already built with floor()
  summarise(films = n(), avg_gross = mean(gross)) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_gross))

decade_avg
Checkpoint (backup data): the 1990s lead on average (one film, Titanic, at $2.26B), then the 2000s (~$1.71B), then the 2020s (~$1.69B), with the 2010s last (~$1.35B) despite having 32 films. So the answer to the question is no: the decade with the most films has the lowest average. Many films, modest grosses each, versus a few blockbusters.
Candy for the first person who can say why a one-film decade “winning” on average is a weak result. (Averages of one are not averages.)






TipWhat to take from this




The AI’s plan was fine. The code was almost right. The mistake was a single function choice that produced plausible-looking output and passed two of the three checks.
The AI also ignored a constraint: it rebuilt decade even though the template said the column already existed. Re-deriving a column you were given is a red flag.
You caught it by running one step and comparing to something you trusted. That’s the habit.





Optional extension
Ask the AI a new question of your own about films_clean. Good ones: “How many films per year since 2015?” “What share of the total top-50 gross is from films still in theaters?” Run its code step by step and write one sentence on whether the result answers your question.

title: 03 · Wikipedia Tables and AI-Assisted ETV Flows
text:
Troubleshooting
htmltab error: “couldn’t find table” / which didn’t match — Wikipedia changed the page. Try which = 1 (first table on the page), or open the URL in a browser, right-click the table, Inspect, and look at its class. Or use the backup CSV.
htmltab returns a table but the columns look wrong — the table may have a two-row header. Try htmltab(doc = films_url, which = "...", header = 1). Or use the backup CSV; the structure of this activity doesn’t depend on live data.
HTTP error 403 / 429 — Wikipedia is rate-limiting the room’s shared Wi-Fi. Use the backup CSV.
parse_number() error “is.character(x) is not TRUE” — you passed it a column that’s already numeric (this happens with the backup CSV for Year). Use as.numeric() for those; keep parse_number() for the dollar column.
Dagger (†) didn’t match — your file encoding may have mangled it. Run grepl("†", Title) instead, which is the same character written as a Unicode code.
AI code uses %>% or library(tidyverse) — it ignored your constraints. Paste back: “Please follow the constraints: native pipe, individual packages.” If it keeps ignoring them, that itself is useful information about the tool.

title: 03 · Wikipedia Tables and AI-Assisted ETV Flows
text:
Exit task (5 minutes, essential)
On an index card or in a shared doc, write:

A question you could answer with data you can get (any data, not today’s).
Its ETV steps: where would you Extract the data from and with what function? What Transform steps (one or two dplyr verbs) would you need? What Visualization would show the answer?
One AI check: describe, in one sentence, how you confirmed that one AI-generated transformation today was (or wasn’t) correct. Name the specific thing you compared.

Hand it in on your way out. Take candy.







NoteWhat was verified and what wasn’t






Verified on 2026-10-28: the Wikipedia URL, the position of the table as the first wikitable on the page, its displayed column names, and all 50 rows (saved to the backup CSV). The htmltab install command and CRAN archival date (2022-11-11) were checked against the GitHub README and CRAN.
Not tested: the R code was not executed when these materials were generated (no R available in the build environment). The exact column names htmltab returns, in particular whether the Ref column survives, should be confirmed live with names(top_films); the select() line is written to work either way. Checkpoint numbers were computed from the backup CSV with a separate tool.

title: 01 · Start Here: Positron and R
text:
It’s going to be a lot, but we got this.
This first file takes about 10 minutes of the live hour. Its only job is to get you oriented in Positron and make sure the packages we need are ready. The real data work starts in 02_csv_extract_transform_visualize.qmd.

title: 01 · Start Here: Positron and R
section: How R, Positron, and packages fit together
text:
How R, Positron, and packages fit together
Three things that beginners often blur together:








Thing
What it is
Analogy




R
The programming language and the engine that runs your code
The engine of a car


Positron
The app you type in. It shows your files, code, console, data, and plots in one window
The car’s dashboard and steering wheel


Packages
Add-ons written by the R community that give R new functions
Upgrades you bolt onto the car



R can run without Positron (it’s just less pleasant). Positron cannot run R code without R installed. Packages live inside your R installation, not inside Positron.
We will use four packages today, each introduced only when we need it:

readr — reads CSV files into R (Extract)
dplyr — transforms data: select, filter, mutate, group, summarise (Transform)
ggplot2 — makes plots (Visualize)
htmltab — pulls tables out of web pages (Extract, file 03)

These first three are part of the “tidyverse” family. You may see tutorials run library(tidyverse) to load all of them at once (plus about five more). We load them one at a time so you know exactly which package each function comes from.

title: 01 · Start Here: Positron and R
text:
Installing vs. loading a package
This confuses everyone at first, so here is the rule:

Install once per computer. install.packages("readr") downloads the package from CRAN (the official R package repository) onto your hard drive. You do this one time, like installing an app on your phone.
Load once per session. library(readr) opens the package so you can use its functions right now. You do this at the top of every script, every time you start R — like opening the app.

If you see the error could not find function "read_csv", you forgot to load. If you see there is no package called 'readr', you forgot to install.

title: 01 · Start Here: Positron and R
text:
Install the packages
Run this once, in the Console. It will take a minute or two and print a lot of text. That’s normal.
# Standard CRAN installs — run once per computer
install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "remotes"))
Now the special case. htmltab is not currently on CRAN. It was removed from the CRAN repository on 2022-11-11, so install.packages("htmltab") will fail with package 'htmltab' is not available. A volunteer maintains a fork on GitHub, so we install from there using the remotes package, which knows how to download and build a package directly from a GitHub repository:
# htmltab is not on CRAN; install from the maintained GitHub fork
remotes::install_github("htmltab/htmltab")
Why the difference? CRAN packages are pre-checked and pre-built, so install.packages() just downloads a finished file. A GitHub package is raw source code, so remotes::install_github() downloads it, builds it on your computer, and then installs it. The result is the same: a package in your library.






NoteVerified



The install command above was checked against the htmltab/htmltab GitHub README and the CRAN archive page on 2026-10-28. The original repository (crubba/htmltab) is unmaintained; the htmltab/htmltab fork is the one to use.


Checkpoint: run this and you should see four TRUEs:
c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "htmltab") %in% rownames(installed.packages())

title: 01 · Start Here: Positron and R
text:
Load the packages
This goes at the top of every script you write today:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
(We’ll add library(htmltab) in file 03.) If dplyr prints a message about objects being masked from package:stats, ignore it. That’s normal.

title: 01 · Start Here: Positron and R
section: A quick tour of Positron (5 minutes, live)
text:
A quick tour of Positron (5 minutes, live)
Positron is built on the same foundation as VS Code, so if you’ve used that, this will feel familiar. If not, here’s everything you need for today.

Open the workshop folder
File → Open Folder… and choose your unzipped etv-workshop folder. The left sidebar (Explorer) now shows qmd/ and data/. Opening the folder (not just a file) matters: it sets your working directory, which is how R finds data/cafe_orders.csv later.
Checkpoint: in the Console, type getwd() and press Enter. The path printed should end in etv-workshop. If it doesn’t, see Troubleshooting.


Write and save a script

File → New File… → choose R File (or create a file named my_script.R).
Type library(readr) on line 1.
Save with Ctrl+S (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+S (Mac). Name it my_script.R inside the etv-workshop folder.

A script is just a text file of R code. Saving it is how your work survives closing Positron. The Console, by contrast, forgets everything when you quit.


Run code
Put your cursor on a line and press Ctrl+Enter (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Enter (Mac). That line is sent to the Console and runs. Highlight several lines first and the whole selection runs. This is the single most important shortcut today.
Positron also has a Run ▶ button in the top-right of the editor that runs the entire file.


The Console
The Console (bottom panel) is where R lives. You can type directly into it for quick experiments (2 + 2), but anything you want to keep belongs in the script. Code you run from the script shows up here, along with its output and any errors.


Inspect data
When you create a data frame (file 02), it appears in the Variables pane on the right, with its row and column counts. Click the small table icon next to its name to open the Data Explorer, a spreadsheet-like view where you can scroll, sort, and filter without writing code. This is your best friend for checking “did that transformation do what I thought?”


View plots
Plots appear in the Plots pane on the right. Arrows let you flip back to earlier plots; there’s a save button to export.


The pipe |>
You’ll see this symbol constantly today. x |> f() means “take x, then do f() to it.” It lets us write transformations as a readable top-to-bottom recipe:
cafe |>
  filter(category == "Coffee") |>
  summarise(total = sum(quantity))
Read it aloud as: “Take cafe, then keep the Coffee rows, then sum the quantity.” Positron can type it for you with Ctrl+Shift+M (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Shift+M (Mac).






TipNot tested in this build



Keyboard shortcuts are the standard Positron defaults as documented, but weren’t machine-verified. If one doesn’t work, open the Command Palette (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P) and type “Open Keyboard Shortcuts” to look it up.

title: 01 · Start Here: Positron and R
section: The ETV framework in one picture
text:
The ETV framework in one picture
Everything today follows the same three moves:
 EXTRACT                 TRANSFORM                     VISUALIZE
 bring data into R  -->  reshape it to answer     -->  draw the answer
 read_csv()              a specific question           ggplot()
 htmltab()               filter(), mutate(),
                         group_by(), summarise()
The framework starts with a question. The question decides which rows to keep, which columns to compute, and which plot to draw. Without a question, you’re just pushing data around.

title: 01 · Start Here: Positron and R
text:
Troubleshooting
Package install fails with “non-zero exit status” or “compilation failed” Run install.packages("readr", type = "binary") (Windows/Mac). If install_github fails on Windows, you may need Rtools from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/. If it still fails: skip htmltab for today and use the backup CSV in file 03.
install_github says “API rate limit exceeded” Too many people on the same Wi-Fi hit GitHub at once. Wait two minutes and try again, or use the backup CSV.
there is no package called 'remotes' You skipped the first install line. Run install.packages("remotes") first.
R can’t find my file (cannot open file 'data/cafe_orders.csv') Your working directory is wrong. Run getwd(). If it doesn’t end in etv-workshop, use File → Open Folder… and pick the right folder, then restart R (Console menu → Restart R). Or run setwd("/full/path/to/etv-workshop") as a last resort.
Positron shows “No interpreter” or a Python interpreter Click the interpreter selector (top-right) and pick R. If no R appears, R isn’t installed or Positron can’t see it; restart Positron after installing R.
Nothing happens when I press Ctrl/Cmd+Enter Make sure your cursor is in the editor (not the Console) and the file is saved as .R.







NoteInstructor checklist






Bring candy! (for first correct prediction, first fixed error, first plot)
Open with: “It’s going to be a lot, but we got this.”
Project the workshop site and its QR code page (https://gato365.github.io/etv-workshop/qr.html)
Poll: who has R installed? Hands up. Anyone without it: pair with a neighbor or start the R installer now
Poll: who has Positron installed? Hands up. Same fix
Confirm everyone has the zip downloaded and unzipped
Poll: hands up if getwd() ends in etv-workshop. Fix stragglers now, not at minute 20
Poll: hands up if the four-TRUE checkpoint passed. Pair anyone without htmltab with a neighbor for file 03, or point them at the backup CSV
Have data/top_films_backup.csv ready in case Wikipedia or htmltab fails live
Watch the clock: 10 / 25 / 25 split, with wrap-up folded into the last 5 minutes of file 03
Remind: run code in small pieces; check the Data Explorer after every transformation

text:
A beginner’s hour in Positron and R. You’ll bring data in, reshape it to answer one real question, draw the answer, and then use an AI assistant to run the next cycle faster without giving up the checks. Three files, two datasets, one framework.


“It’s going to be a lot, but we got this.” Opening line. Candy is involved.

title: ETV Workshop: Positron + R
text:
The framework



Extract

Bring the data in
From a CSV file or straight out of a Wikipedia table. One package each.
readr::read_csv() · htmltab::htmltab()





Transform

Reshape it to the question
Keep what matters, fix what’s broken, group and summarise. Always with |>.
select() · filter() · mutate() · group_by() · summarise()





Visualize

Draw the answer
One clearly labeled chart whose title states the finding, not the variables.
ggplot() + geom_col() + labs(title = "the answer")

title: ETV Workshop: Positron + R
text:
Before you arrive
Installs take 10–15 minutes and eat the hour if done live. Please finish these first. Full details are in file 01.


Pre-workshop checklist

Install R 4.2 or newer from cloud.r-project.org (or with rig). Positron does not include R.
Install Positron from positron.posit.co.
Open Positron once and confirm the interpreter selector (top-right) shows R 4.x.
Run the package installs on the right in the Console. Say yes to prompts.
Download the zip above, unzip it, and in Positron use File → Open Folder… on the etv-workshop folder.

Candy for the first correct prediction, the first fixed error, and the first plot.


Package installs (once per computer)
# From CRAN
install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "remotes"))

# htmltab was removed from CRAN on 2022-11-11,
# so it installs from the maintained GitHub fork:
remotes::install_github("htmltab/htmltab")

# Checkpoint: four TRUEs
c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "htmltab") %in%
  rownames(installed.packages())
Install once; load with library() at the top of every script.

title: ETV Workshop: Positron + R
text:
If something breaks
The four failures that eat workshop time. Each file has a longer troubleshooting list.
cannot open file 'data/cafe_orders.csv' Wrong working directory. Run getwd(); it should end in etv-workshop. Use File → Open Folder… on that folder, then restart R.
package 'htmltab' is not available Expected: it isn’t on CRAN. Use remotes::install_github("htmltab/htmltab"). If GitHub rate-limits the room, skip it and use top_films_backup.csv.
could not find function "read_csv" The package is installed but not loaded this session. Run library(readr). Same fix for dplyr and ggplot2 functions.
htmltab: table not found / columns look wrong Wikipedia changed the page. Try which = 1, or read the backup CSV; the column names match, so the rest of the code runs unchanged.






NoteAbout the code in these files





R code follows current readr, dplyr, and ggplot2 documentation but was not executed when these materials were built; expected outputs were computed from the CSVs separately. Each file lists what was and wasn’t tested.

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
text:
A campus café wants to know where its money comes from.

Which drink category brings in the most revenue, and is that because it sells more drinks or pricier drinks?

Everything in this file serves that one question. Before touching any code, write down your prediction:






TipPredict first



Three categories: Coffee, Tea, Specialty (mochas, frappes, hot chocolate). Which one do you think brings in the most total money? Which one do you think has the highest revenue per order? Write both guesses on paper. Candy for the closest.

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
text:
The data
File: data/cafe_orders.csv · 506 rows · 10 columns






WarningSynthetic data



This dataset is simulated for teaching. It was generated with a random-number seed to look like four weeks of orders (Sept 21 – Oct 18, 2026) at a fictional campus café. No real business is represented. The quirks are deliberate.





Column
Type (as stored)
Meaning




order_id
number
Unique order number


date
date (YYYY-MM-DD)
Day of the order


day_of_week
text
Monday … Sunday


hour
number
Hour of day, 24-hour clock (7 = 7 am, 13 = 1 pm)


drink
text
Specific drink name


category
text
Coffee, Tea, or Specialty


size
text
Small, Medium, Large


price
text
Price of one drink, stored like "$4.75"


quantity
number
How many of that drink in the order


loyalty_member
text
yes / no



Notice the price column. It has a dollar sign, so R will read it as text, not as a number. You can’t add up text. Fixing that is our cleaning task.

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
text:
Set up your script
Create a new R file in your etv-workshop folder, save it as cafe_etv.R, and start with the packages:
library(readr)    # Extract: read CSV files
library(dplyr)    # Transform: filter, mutate, group, summarise
library(ggplot2)  # Visualize: make plots
Run those three lines (Ctrl/Cmd+Enter on each, or highlight all and run). Then confirm R can see the data folder:
getwd()                    # should end in "etv-workshop"
file.exists("data/cafe_orders.csv")   # should print TRUE
If that prints FALSE, stop and fix it (see Troubleshooting in file 01). Nothing else works until this is TRUE.

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
text:
EXTRACT — bring the data in
read_csv() from readr reads the file and gives it a name in R. We’ll call it cafe.
cafe <- read_csv("data/cafe_orders.csv")
Checkpoint: the Console prints a summary like:
Rows: 506 Columns: 10
── Column specification ──────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (6): day_of_week, drink, category, size, price, loyalty_member
dbl  (3): order_id, hour, quantity
date (1): date
Three things to notice:

chr means character (text), dbl means double (a number with decimals), date means readr recognized the date format.
price is listed under chr. That’s our problem.
cafe now appears in the Variables pane. Click the table icon to open it in the Data Explorer and scroll around. Get a feel for it.

Two quick ways to look at the data in code:
glimpse(cafe)   # one line per column: name, type, first few values
head(cafe)      # first 6 rows
glimpse() is from dplyr and is the fastest way to answer “what did I just load?”

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
section: TRANSFORM — step 1: pick the columns that matter
text:
TRANSFORM — step 1: pick the columns that matter
Our question needs category, price, and quantity. We’ll keep drink too, for context. select() chooses columns:
cafe |>
  select(drink, category, price, quantity)
Run it. The Console shows a 506 × 4 table. We didn’t save this anywhere (no <-), so cafe is unchanged. That’s a good habit: look first, save later.

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
text:
TRANSFORM — step 2: the cleaning task
We need to turn "$4.75" into 4.75. readr has a function built for exactly this: parse_number() strips out everything that isn’t part of a number and returns the number.
parse_number("$4.75")       # try it: returns 4.75
parse_number("$1,234.50")   # also handles commas: 1234.5
The decision: we could instead edit the CSV by hand and delete the dollar signs. We don’t, for two reasons. First, 506 rows is tedious and 50,000 would be impossible. Second, and more important, if the café sends us next month’s file, our script fixes it automatically. Clean in code, not in the file.
mutate() from dplyr creates new columns (or overwrites existing ones). We’ll make price_num and, while we’re there, revenue for each order:
cafe_clean <- cafe |>
  mutate(
    price_num = parse_number(price),
    revenue   = price_num * quantity
  )
This time we saved the result as cafe_clean because we’ll build on it.
Checkpoint: verify it worked.
glimpse(cafe_clean)
You should now see 12 columns: price_num as dbl and revenue as dbl. Check a few values make sense:
cafe_clean |>
  select(price, price_num, quantity, revenue) |>
  head()
A $5.75 drink with quantity 1 should show revenue 5.75. A $5.00 drink with quantity 2 should show 10.00. If price_num is full of NA, something went wrong; ask for help.
One more sanity check, because it catches typos in the data that would otherwise silently poison every result:
summary(cafe_clean$price_num)
Minimum should be 2.50, maximum 7.00, no NAs. A minimum of 0 or a maximum of 475 would mean a price was mistyped in the source.

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
text:
TRANSFORM — step 3: group and summarise
Now the heart of the question. group_by() splits the data into one group per category; summarise() collapses each group into one row of totals.
cafe_summary <- cafe_clean |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(
    orders        = n(),
    total_revenue = sum(revenue),
    avg_revenue   = mean(revenue)
  )

cafe_summary
Checkpoint: three rows.
  category  orders total_revenue avg_revenue
  <chr>      <int>         <dbl>       <dbl>
1 Coffee       276         1612         5.84
2 Specialty    126          919.        7.29
3 Tea          104          562.        5.40
(Your digits may display with slightly different rounding; the values are the same.)
Stop and read the table. Compare it to your prediction. Coffee makes the most total money. But Specialty makes the most per order, by a lot. That’s already most of the answer.






NoteWhy n()?



n() counts the rows in each group. It takes no arguments. It only works inside summarise() or mutate() after a group_by().

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
text:
VISUALIZE — draw the answer
A plot should make the answer visible in two seconds. For “which category makes the most?” a bar chart is right.
ggplot2 builds plots in layers. First you say what data and which columns map to which axes (aesthetics). Then you add a layer that says how to draw them (geom_col for bars whose heights are already computed).
ggplot(cafe_summary, aes(x = category, y = total_revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a6f4e") +
  labs(
    title    = "Coffee brings in the most total revenue",
    subtitle = "Four weeks of simulated café orders, Sept 21 – Oct 18, 2026",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Total revenue (USD)",
    caption  = "Synthetic data for the ETV Workshop"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
Notice the title is the answer, not a description like “Revenue by Category.” Make every plot title state what the viewer should take away.
Checkpoint: the Plots pane shows three bars; Coffee is clearly tallest (around 1,600), Specialty in the middle (around 900), Tea shortest (around 560).






NoteWhy + and not |>?



ggplot2 was written before the pipe existed, and it stacks layers onto a plot rather than passing data through steps. So inside a ggplot you use +. Everywhere else today, use |>. If you mix them up, ggplot gives a helpful error telling you so.



Second chart, same two lines changed
The question also asked why. Swap the y-axis to avg_revenue and the story flips:
ggplot(cafe_summary, aes(x = category, y = avg_revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#b5562a") +
  labs(
    title = "…but Specialty drinks make the most per order",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Average revenue per order (USD)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
text:
Change something and try again
Pick one of these and run it. Predict the result before you run it. Then check the Data Explorer or the printed table to see if you were right.
A. Swap the grouping variable. Change group_by(category) to group_by(size). Which size brings in the most money? (Does the answer surprise you given that Large costs the most?)
B. Add a filter. Insert filter(hour < 12) |> right after cafe_clean |> so you only look at morning orders. Does Coffee’s lead grow or shrink in the morning?
C. Two grouping variables. Change to group_by(category, loyalty_member). Do loyalty members spend more per order in every category, or just some?
# Template: copy, then change ONE thing
cafe_clean |>
  # filter(hour < 12) |>              # <- option B: uncomment
  group_by(category) |>               # <- option A or C: change this
  summarise(
    orders        = n(),
    total_revenue = sum(revenue),
    avg_revenue   = mean(revenue)
  )
Every one of these is the same ETV recipe with one ingredient changed. That’s the skill: not memorizing functions, but knowing which step of the recipe your question lives in.

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
section: Interpretation — answering the question in plain language
text:
Interpretation — answering the question in plain language

Coffee brings in the most total revenue, about $1,612 over four weeks, roughly $700 more than Specialty and nearly three times Tea. But that lead comes from volume, not price: Coffee accounts for 276 of the 506 orders (55%). Per order, Specialty drinks earn the most, about $7.29 versus $5.84 for Coffee and $5.40 for Tea. So the honest answer to the café is: coffee pays the bills because people buy a lot of it, while specialty drinks are the most valuable individual sale. If the café wants to raise revenue without raising prices, nudging coffee customers toward a specialty drink is the lever these data point to.

Notice how the interpretation mentions actual numbers, says what the data can and can’t tell us, and ends with what someone could do about it. That’s the finish line for every ETV cycle.

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
section: Optional extensions (skip if short on time)
text:
Optional extensions (skip if short on time)
Daily revenue over time. Group by date instead, then plot with geom_line() and aes(x = date, y = total_revenue). Weekends should be visibly lower.
Top drinks. group_by(drink) then arrange(desc(total_revenue)) then head(5). arrange() sorts; desc() reverses the order.
A reusable recipe. Put your whole pipeline (read → mutate → group → summarise → plot) into one script and run it top to bottom with the ▶ button. If it runs clean from an empty session, you’ve written a real, reproducible analysis.

title: 02 · Café Orders: Extract → Transform → Visualize
text:
Troubleshooting
Error: object 'cafe' not found — you skipped the read_csv() line or it failed. Scroll up in the Console for the real error.
could not find function "read_csv" — you didn’t run library(readr). Loading packages is per session; if you restarted R, run the three library() lines again.
price_num is all NA — most likely you wrote parse_number(price_num) instead of parse_number(price), or the CSV was edited in Excel and saved with a different encoding. Re-download the CSV.
The plot pane is blank / the plot is tiny — drag the pane divider to make the Plots pane bigger, or click the “open in new window” icon.
Error in ggplot(...) : could not find function "ggplot" — run library(ggplot2).







NoteNot tested in this build





The R code in this file follows current readr/dplyr/ggplot2 documentation and the expected outputs were computed from the CSV with a separate tool, but the R code itself was not executed when these materials were generated. If an output differs slightly in formatting (column widths, rounding), that’s expected. If a function errors, check the package version with packageVersion("dplyr") (should be 1.1 or newer).
